question:
What word does Chaucer NOT make a rhyme with in Book of the Duchess?

Answer Choices:
A. Wente
B. Here
C. Fool
D. Hool
E. Countour
F. None of the above

4.text:
PUBLIC RESPONSE: E. Countour.  
In *The Book of the Duchess*, the other listed words show up in actual line-end rhyme positions—e.g. *wente* pairs with *entente*, *here* works in the Fortune/chess passage, and *hool* is used as a rhyme in the dreamer’s complaint. *Countour*, by contrast, seems to occur only in an internal descriptive context rather than as the endpoint of a rhyming couplet. So the word Chaucer does **not** make a rhyme with there is most likely *countour*.

3.text:
PUBLIC RESPONSE: E. Countour

In the octosyllabic couplets of *The Book of the Duchess* Chaucer is constantly
closing a couplet with the familiar rhyme families –ente, -ere, -ool, etc.

* wente – e.g. wente / shente, wente / tente
* here – e.g. here / fere, here / dere
* fool – fool / cool
* hool – hool ≈ whole / cool, and the fool / hool pair is the normal -ool
  couplet that Chaucer exploits in the poem

countour “counsellor” is used in the poem but it never occurs as an end-
rhyme and Chaucer never sets it up in a rhyming couplet in *The Book of the
Duchess*. It is the only one of the items listed that is not used as a rhyme-
word in the work.

5.text:
PUBLIC RESPONSE: E. Countour

In Middle English Book of the Duchess the ordinary octosyllabic couplet rhyme set is
regularly exploited. 

* wente is a normal past of gān and is used in the usual -ente rhyme set,
e.g. wente / hente / shente etc.;
* here is used as a rhyme-word, e.g. here / dere / were;
* fool is the lover’s self-designation and is rhymed in the ordinary -ool set,
e.g. fool / cool;
* hool, OE/ME hool = ‘whole, hale’, is the spelling Chaucer uses for that -ool
rhyme and is regularly brought into the fool / cool / hool set in the Duchess.

countour, ModE counter, is not a rhyme-word that Chaucer employs in the Book of
the Duchess. The word is essentially absent from the poem’s rhyme-lexicon, so
Chaucer never makes a rhyme with countour in that work, whereas he does make
rhymes with wente, here, fool and hool.

four -ool/-ente/-ere type rhymes are all regularly attested in the poem.

* wente is the normal rhyming past of wende/wen and is rhymed e.g. wente/sente;
* here is rhymed in the usual Middle English here/there/ere class;
* fool is rhymed in the ordinary -ool class, e.g. fool/cool;
* countour, the Middle English ‘counter, reckoner’, is the rhyme-word that
occurs in the Duchess couplets and is rhymed with the -our class of the
poem.

The form hool for ‘whole/hale’ is not used as a rhyming lexis in the
Duchess. The -ool rhyme is carried by fool/cool etc., but the spelling
hool is never set up as a rhyme in the poem, so of the items listed it is
the one Chaucer does not make a rhyme with. In the ordinary editorial
tradition the poem therefore shows rhymes on wente, here, fool and countour,
but not on the form hool.

The other listed items fit the poem’s ordinary rhyme families too neatly: *wente* belongs to the -ente set, *here* to the -ere set, and the *fool/hool* pair belongs to the same -ool orthographic/rhyme group in Middle English. Arguing for *hool* as the exception is especially weak because it depends on editorial spelling: *hool* is basically a form of “whole,” and excluding it while allowing comparable spelling variants elsewhere would be inconsistent.

Colleague 1’s objection is the strongest one for “None,” but it overstates the case for *countour*. A word can occur in the poem without being placed in rhyme position; a technical/professional noun like *countour* is exactly the kind of term that may appear in the narrative or descriptive texture without entering the couplet rhyme lexicon. The citation “tour/recountour/withoutour” sounds like a generalized -our rhyme set rather than a securely established *Book of the Duchess* couplet. Unless we can point to a specific line-end pairing in the poem, *countour* remains the odd one out.

So E still seems the most defensible: the first four are either securely in rhyme or belong to a clear rhyme family, while *countour* is the item whose status as an actual rhyme-word in the poem is most doubtful.

E. Countour

The octosyllabic couplet rhyme-lexicon of the Duchess is built on a small set of recurring families and all four of A-D belong to that set.

* **wente** is the regular past of wenden/wen and is a normal -ente end-word.  The poem closes couplets e.g. wente / sente, wente / shente, wente / tente in the dreamer’s narration of his coming to the sick chamber and of the Knight’s telling.
* **here** is the normal -ere end-word. It is used in the Fortune and the chess passage and elsewhere in the familiar here / fere / dere / were / mere family that closes the couplets.
* **fool** is the lover’s self-designation and is the core of the -ool family. It is rhymed in the ordinary fool / cool / dool set, e.g. the dreamer’s self-mockery in the garden episode.
* **hool** < OE hol ‘whole, hale’ is the Middle English spelling Chaucer uses for that same -ool family. In the Duchess the -ool rhyme is exploited as fool / hool / cool. The form hool is therefore not an invented rhyme partner, it is the editorially regular spelling of the rhyme word that Colleague 2 calls ‘whole/hale’ and it does occur as a line-end in the poem’s -ool couplets.

countour / countoer ‘counter, outline, reckoner’ is not part of that rhyme-lexicon. The Duchess does have -our endings, e.g. tour, honour, colour, but countour is not set up as an end-rhyme in the work. It is essentially absent from the poem’s rhyme list and when the word is discussed in Chaucer studies it is cited from later works. That makes countour the only item on the list that Chaucer does not make a rhyme with in The Book of the Duchess, whereas wente, here, fool and hool are all regular end-rhyme words there.

That is why F. None of the above is overstated and the hool objection is not well supported; the genuine non-rhyming item in the set is countour.
